Geoeconomic Fragmentation and Supply Chain Re-Shoring: Macroeconomic Impacts

Working Paper WP/25/182 | Published October 18, 2025 | Research Directorate

The Rise of Geoeconomic Fragmentation

The post-Cold War era of hyper-globalized multilateral supply chains is undergoing a structural realignment toward geoeconomic fragmentation. Strategic policies promoting "friend-shoring" and domestic "re-shoring" have surged as advanced economies prioritize national security, supply resilience, and strategic autonomy over pure Ricardian comparative advantage and cost minimization.

Our computable general equilibrium (CGE) econometric simulations indicate that severe fragmentation into competing geopolitical trading blocs could reduce long-term global gross domestic product (GDP) by between 1.2% and 1.8%, with emerging markets and developing economies bearing disproportionate output losses up to 4.2%.

Inflationary Pressures and Capital Misallocation

Re-shoring complex manufacturing stages inevitably exerts upward pressure on baseline consumer price inflation. Relocating labor-intensive assembly processes to advanced domestic economies encounters substantial wage differentials, where manufacturing compensation often exceeds $32 per hour compared to $5.50 to $7.20 per hour in Southeast Asian export hubs.

Furthermore, duplicative capital expenditure investments in parallel semiconductor fabrication plants and clean energy hardware facilities reduce aggregate capital efficiency. Central banks face higher structural neutral real interest rates (r-star) as supply-side frictions become permanent features of global commerce.

Policy Recommendations

Multilateral institutions urge policymakers to pursue a "narrow yard, high fence" strategy: ring-fencing genuinely critical dual-use technologies while preserving open, non-discriminatory trade in non-sensitive goods and intermediate agricultural inputs to avoid compounding global inflationary headwinds.
